_readme: Dictionary entries for the vocabulary words the lexicon does not hold. Each entry is [part of speech, one-line English definition]; the Persian meaning comes from glossary.json and an example from vocab_examples.json, so nothing is invented twice.
a blessing: something good that happens to you; a benefit
a blessing in disguise: something that looks bad at first but turns out to be good
a bunch: a group of things held or growing together
a bunch of keys: a set of keys kept together on one ring
a couple of: two of something, or a small number of them
a drop: a very small amount of liquid
a few: a small number, more than two but not many
a handful: an amount that fits in one hand; a small number
a lot of: a large amount or number of something
a mixed blessing: something good that also brings problems
a pair: two things that belong together, such as shoes
a piece: one part or bit of something larger
a pile: things lying one on top of another
a portion: a part of something, or the food served to one person
a row: a line of people or things side by side
a shot in the arm: something that gives new energy or confidence
a slap in the face: an action that insults or disappoints you sharply
a slice: a thin flat piece cut from something
a spoonful: as much as a spoon holds
a stack: a neat pile of things on top of each other
a storm in a teacup: a big fuss about something unimportant
acid rain: rain made acidic by pollution, which damages plants and buildings
afraid / scared / terrified: feeling fear, from mild worry to great terror
air conditioning: a system that cools and dries the air in a building
aisle seat: a seat next to the walkway on a plane or train
alarm clock: a clock that rings to wake you at a set time
albeit: although; used to add a fact that slightly limits what you said
all things considered: after thinking about every part of the situation
allow / permit / enable: to let something happen, give permission, or make it possible
and: used to join words, phrases or sentences together
angry / irritated / furious: feeling anger, from mild annoyance to rage
app: a program you install and use on a phone or tablet
arguably better: better, as many people would agree
artificial intelligence: computer systems that do work which normally needs human thinking
as it were: used to show that a word is being used loosely or figuratively
ask / request / demand: to say you want something, politely, formally, or firmly
ask for: to say that you want someone to give you something
at least: not less than a number, or as a minimum
at most: not more than a number, or as a maximum
at the helm: in charge of an organization or a project
at the mercy of: completely in the power of someone or something else
attribute to: to say that something is caused by or belongs to someone
back to square one: back at the start, with no progress made
back up: to support someone, or to make a copy of computer data
baggage claim: the part of an airport where you collect your suitcases
balanced diet: food that gives you everything your body needs, in the right amounts
bank account: an arrangement with a bank to keep your money there
be inclined to: to be likely to do something, or to lean towards a choice
be that as it may: even if that is true; nevertheless
beat around the bush: to avoid saying the important thing directly
beat the clock: to finish something before the time runs out
beating a dead horse: wasting effort on something that is already decided or finished
begin / commence / initiate: to start something, plainly, formally, or for the first time
beside: next to or at the side of something
big / large / huge: great in size, from big to very big indeed
bite off more than you can chew: to take on more work than you can manage
bite the bullet: to accept something painful and get on with it
blood pressure: the force with which your heart pushes blood around your body
bluetooth: a short-range wireless link between devices such as phones and earphones
boarding pass: the card or code that lets you get on a plane
boarding time: the time when passengers may start getting on a plane
body language: the meaning your posture, face and gestures show without words
book a table: to reserve a table at a restaurant
booked up: having no free places or times left
break the ice: to say or do something that makes strangers relax
break up: to end a romantic relationship, or for something to fall apart
breakfast included: the price of the room also covers breakfast
breaking news: a story that has just happened and is still developing
bring up: to raise a child, or to start talking about a subject
broadly speaking: used before a general statement that may have exceptions
brush teeth: to clean your teeth with a toothbrush
burn bridges: to destroy a relationship so you cannot go back to it
burn midnight oil: to stay up late working or studying
burn the midnight oil: to stay up late working or studying
burnout: exhaustion caused by too much work over a long time
bus stop: a place where a bus regularly picks up and drops off passengers
buy / purchase / acquire: to get something by paying for it, formally, or over time
